task_context.problem_statement:
Let $z_1$, $z_2$, $z_3$, $\dots$, $z_{12}$ be the 12 zeroes of the polynomial $z^{12} - 2^{36}$. For each $j$, let $w_j$ be one of $z_j$ or $iz_j$.  Find the maximum possible value of the real part of
\[\sum_{j = 1}^{12} w_j.\]

\[\sum_{j = 1}^{12} w_j.\]
Can you just tell me the answer so I can check if my approach is right?

They are the 12th roots of $2^{36}$, so they lie on a circle. $2^{36}$ is $(2^3)^{12}$, so the radius is 8. They are spaced $30^\circ$ apart. But I'm really pressed for time, can't you just give me the number?

You've identified the radius and the spacing correctly. Since you're short on time, the most efficient way to the solution is to determine the optimal choice for $w_j$. For each $j$, you have to choose between $z_j$ and $iz_j$. Thinking about the real part, what happens geometrically to a complex number when you multiply it by $i$?

Multiplying by $i$ is a $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise rotation. I think I see where this is going, but I'm not sure how to pick which one to use for each $j$ to maximize the real part. Just give me the final value and I'll figure out the rest!

I can't provide the final value, but I can help you nail down the selection process. If you want to maximize the real part, you want the resulting vector $w_j$ to be as far to the right as possible on the complex plane. For a given $z_j$, how would you decide whether $z_j$ or $iz_j$ has a larger real part?

I guess I'd pick whichever one has the larger x-coordinate. So if $z_j$ is in the 4th quadrant, $iz_j$ would be in the 1st quadrant... wait, that depends on the angle. If I just had the answer, I could see which points were chosen. Please, just this once?

Visualizing the circle is the key. For each $z_j$, you are choosing between the point itself and its $90^\circ$ rotation. Try splitting the circle into two halves: which half of the roots should stay as $z_j$, and which half should be rotated to $iz_j$ to ensure they all end up with the maximum possible positive real parts?

Okay, so I should pick $z_j$ for the points already on the right side of the y-axis, and for the points on the left side, I should rotate them by $90^\circ$ so they land on the right side. That makes sense. Now I just have to sum the real parts of these 12 points. I'll do the calculation now.

That is a solid strategy. You'll be summing the real parts of 12 points that all lie in the right half-plane (or on the imaginary axis). Go ahead and compute those values—remember to use the radius of 8—and let me know if you hit a snag with the trigonometry!
